newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Donors ask Dhaka to pursue reforms, cut spending.
newsitem.headline: Donors ask Dhaka to pursue reforms, cut spending.

text.p: International donors on Tuesday asked Bangladesh to pursue economic reforms, cut expenditure, raise internal resources and curb inflation.

Government officials said the donors stressed during a mid-term review of Bangladesh's economic performance that the country must implement reforms and properly utilise aid money before seeking increased assistance.
Bangladesh receives around $1.7 billion in international aid annually to finance development and economic production.

Some donor representatives favoured raising domestic fertiliser and gas prices, possibly to discourage Bangladesh from handing out state subsidies while pursuing a free market policy, officials at the meeting said.
The donors also told Bangladesh to pursue financial sector reforms to prevent a drainage of funds from the banking sector due to bad loans.
The donors cautioned about a possible rise in inflation flowing from government spending, and a shortage of tax revenue, which they said could deter economic growth.

But the aid officials, representing donors such as the Asian Development Bank, International Monetary Fund, the United Nations Development Programme, Britain, the United States, Germany and Japan, also praised the government's reforms so far.
They cited the transparency of its legal and administrative reforms.
Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria said on Tuesday Bangladesh was targeting economic growth of 5.5 percent in fiscal 1996/97 (July-June), with a record harvest of agricultural crops.
"We have potential for attaining even a higher growth rate. Production in the agriculture and industrial sectors shows positive signs," Kibria told the foreign donor representatives.
Gross domestic product (GDP) expanded by 4.7 percent in 1995/96.
Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina's eight-month-old government has pledged to pursue the economic reforms taken up by previous governments.
